title: Federation Army: How Much to Merge?
sources: Constitutional Agreement of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 18 March 1994
content:
The Washington Agreement of March 1994 established the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina on paper and charged a Federation Army to integrate the ARBiH and the HVO into a unified military structure. Six months on, the institutional reality lagged the paper architecture. UNPROFOR and ICRC field reports recorded persistent dual command: ARBiH corps and HVO operative zones operating side by side, coordinating against the VRS where interests aligned but answering to separate staffs, separate logistics, and separate political masters in Sarajevo and Mostar.

For the Sarajevo command the integration question was genuinely fraught. Full merger would have ended the recent Croat-Bosniak war institutionally and pooled scarce manpower and materiel for the coming offensives — but it required trusting a former enemy with command authority over Bosniak formations and surrendering the ARBiH's autonomous character. Parallel commands preserved that autonomy at the cost of friction, duplicated effort, and the constant risk that the Federation existed only on paper.

Historically the Federation Army remained largely a parallel-commands arrangement through 1994 and into 1995: real coordination in the field, especially around Bihać and in the central-Bosnian offensives, but no genuine unified command structure. The deeper merger envisioned at Washington never materialized before Dayton.

The posture recorded here conditions how effectively Federation forces could mass for the 1995 offensives — and how durable the Croat-Bosniak reconciliation proved under operational stress.
